blanks.sentence: In Britain, about _____ of adults are estimated to weigh more than the healthy range.
Drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro are adapted forms of _____ found in the body.
These medicines copy the body’s signal that makes people feel _____ for longer.
After taking Mounjaro, one listener lost _____ within half a year.
She said she no longer felt hungry, so the repeated mental pressure around eating, known as _____, stopped.
A long-term inner argument about food harmed her _____.
These medicines were first developed to treat _____, not to reduce body weight.
This condition is linked to excessively high _____.
Weight loss was first noticed as a _____ of the diabetes medication.
UK public health advice suggests the drugs should not replace a _____.

multipleChoice.question: What problem is introduced before the discussion of weight loss drugs?
options: Exercise routines are becoming less popular among adults.
Healthy habits do not help everyone maintain a healthy weight.
Most British adults refuse to change their eating habits.
New medicines have made diet and exercise unnecessary.

multipleChoice.question: How are the drugs said to support weight loss?
options: They increase the amount of exercise people can do.
They remove sugar from food before it is digested.
They permanently change the body’s natural hormones.
They extend the feeling of fullness so people eat less.

multipleChoice.question: What change is reported in the listener’s experience with Mounjaro?
options: She lost a substantial amount of weight and felt more positive about it.
She stopped taking the medicine after six months because of hunger.
She became unsure whether the drug had any real effect.
She used the drug mainly to improve her running performance.

multipleChoice.question: In this context, what does “food noise” mainly refer to?
options: The physical sound made while preparing meals.
A medical warning that food has too much sugar.
Unwanted thoughts and judgement connected with eating.
A strict diet plan that tells people what not to eat.

multipleChoice.question: What does the “angel and devil” image suggest about her relationship with food?
options: She enjoyed choosing between two equally healthy diets.
She experienced a repeated internal struggle over eating.
She believed other people were controlling her meals.
She wanted to eat only foods that were considered forbidden.

multipleChoice.question: What long-term effect did this inner conflict have?
options: It made her more disciplined about daily exercise.
It encouraged her to study nutrition professionally.
It helped her separate hunger from temptation.
It weakened her confidence in herself over many years.

multipleChoice.question: What contrast is made about the original purpose of these medicines?
options: They were first intended for diabetes, not weight loss.
They were first sold for obesity, then withdrawn for diabetes.
They were created for mental health before being used for appetite.
They were designed as lifestyle products rather than medical treatments.

multipleChoice.question: What did doctors notice when the diabetes medicine was used?
options: Patients needed a higher dose of insulin.
Patients stopped experiencing all side effects.
Patients were also losing weight.
Patients no longer needed any medical advice.

multipleChoice.question: In the explanation, why is the side effect described as unusual in this case?
options: It was impossible for doctors to observe it at first.
It was normally undesirable, but here it helped patients.
It had no connection with the medicine’s original use.
It affected only people who did not have diabetes.

multipleChoice.question: What caution is given near the end of the discussion?
options: Medication should be combined with broader healthy-living support.
People should avoid using these drugs under all circumstances.
The drugs have been proven to solve obesity by themselves.
Public health officials believe lifestyle advice is no longer useful.
